formula: Sales ~ month(Date) + as.numeric(Date - as.Date('2013-01-01')) + Promo + SchoolHoliday + StateHoliday + CompetitionDistance + CompetitionOpenSinceMonth + CompetitionOpenSinceYear + Promo2 + Promo2SinceWeek + Promo2SinceYear + PromoInterval + StoreType + Assortment + (1 | Store) + (0 + as.numeric(Date - as.Date('2013-01-01')) | Store) + (0 + I(as.numeric(Date - as.Date('2013-01-01'))^2) | Store)
notes: RULE GAP: the documented model fits a store x month aggregate, and its time terms are expressions of the datetime column Date, which is ignored since the contract codes no datetime covariate; the random slopes on t and t^2 stay in the formula only. Read: Simchoni and Rosset (LMMNN, arXiv 2206.03314) Sec. 5.2.2 and Table 8 (Rossmann: 1.1K stores, 25-31 monthly measures, "Total $ sales (in 100K)", "random terms in t up to a quadratic with no correlations between these terms"); Sigrist 2023 Table 1 and run_experiments.R ((1 |Store) + (0 + t|Store) + (0 + I(t^2)|Store), gpboost with uncorrelated slopes); LMMNN's lme4 baseline (r_scripts/lme4_on_datasets/lme4_rossmann.R) writes (1 + t + I(t^2)|Store), correlated. Preprocessing (rossmann_etl.R in both repositories): daily sales summed per store and month and divided by 1e5, Open, Promo, SchoolHoliday and the StateHoliday dummies summed per month, store data imputed by medians (PromoInterval NA as a level), t = days since 2013-01-01 over its maximum; on this daily table the terms are the same columns per day. BeyondArena keeps open days only and drops Open and Customers; its task has no group_on. DayOfWeek is not a documented term.
call: The documented model fits monthly sales per store with uncorrelated random slopes per store on time t and t², but this table is daily and holds time only as the date column Date. The reading writes the slopes as expressions of Date in the formula only and leaves random_slopes blank. Should they be in both fields, in the formula only, or in neither?

notes: RULE GAP: a Gaussian-process spatial random effect has no lme4 form; the county indexes it, so State:County groups (County names repeat across states). Read: Simchoni and Rosset (LMMNN, arXiv 2206.03314) Sec. 5.2.3, Table 10 (Income: 71K tracts, 1-2K per location, p = 30, "3K US counties", "Ann. income $ (log)") and Appendix 4 Table 31; r_scripts/ETL/us_income_etl.R and notebooks/spatial/us_income.ipynb (mode spatial, q_spatial = the counties, two spatial variance parameters, no grouped random effect). A further documented GLMM (Sec. 6, lme4_cars_glmm.R: glmer(I(long west of a cut) ~ covariates + price + (1 | model_id), binomial)) takes a recode of long as its response and is not filed. region and state are not documented terms.
call: The documented model has a random intercept per car model and a Gaussian process over the listing coordinates, which lme4 syntax cannot write, so the formula states both in words and grouping_factors holds model and lat:long. Should the row keep the process in words, write it as a random intercept per lat:long, or leave the spatial effect out?

formula: nWBV ~ `MR Delay` + Age + `M/F` + Group + `MR Delay`:Group + (1 + `MR Delay` | `Subject ID`)
notes: OASIS-2 longitudinal (Marcus et al. 2010, J Cogn Neurosci 22:2677; Mendeley tsy6rbc5d4): 150 subjects aged 60 to 96, each scanned on two or more visits at least a year apart, 373 sessions; Group is nondemented, demented or converted. BeyondArena's dementia_prediction (Table B.1: grouped multiclass) predicts Group grouped by subject, but Group is fixed per subject, so it carries no random effect. The paper follows nWBV, normalized whole-brain volume, across visits: per-subject atrophy slopes compared by age, sex and dementia status with analysis of covariance (section Estimated Total Intracranial Volume and Normalized Whole-brain Volume, Fig. 3). Rendered as a random intercept and MR Delay slope per subject with the slope differing by Group; no mixed model published. MRI ID, Visit, Hand (all right-handed), CDR and MMSE (the ratings Group is built from), eTIV and ASF (the normalization behind nWBV) are ignored; EDUC and SES stay usable.
call: BeyondArena predicts Group, which is constant within a subject, and Marcus et al. (2010) follow normalized whole-brain volume nWBV across visits. Is nWBV, with a random intercept and an MR Delay slope per subject, a documented model of this table, or should the row take another response or none?

RT, SPORDER, ADJINC and the person weights are ignored, PUBCOV and ESR as the other tasks' responses. Food Stamps (FS), TableShift's fourth ACS task, is a housing-record variable not in this file. formula: I((math + read)/2) ~ I(students/teachers) + english + lunch + calworks + (1 | county)
notes: RULE GAP: the documented response is score = (math + read)/2, which is no column, so response names math, the formula holds the mean and read is ignored. Read CASchools.Rd and StockWatson2007.Rd: Stock and Watson (2007) fit lm(score ~ stratio + english + lunch + calworks) (Table 7.1, col. 5, the page's fmc5), stratio = students/teachers, with sandwich standard errors and no grouping. The 420 K-6 and K-8 districts repeat within California counties (county, a factor with many levels), so county is filed as the grouping factor, a cluster the source treats as independent; the random intercept is the reader's proposal. teachers only scales students and is ignored as a denominator; district and school are ids; grades, computer, expenditure and income are not in this model.
call: Stock and Watson's response is the district's average test score, (math + read)/2, which no column holds. The reading names math as the response, writes the average as the formula's left side and ignores read; Ecdat's Star instead files each summed score as a row of its own. Is a response computed from two columns a response of this table, and if so, should the row model the average or each score?

formula: tmathssk ~ classk + totexpk + sex + freelunk + race + (1 | schidkn)
notes: Project STAR kindergarten, students in schools (schidkn, the school indicator). The help page cites Stock and Watson (2003), Introduction to Econometrics, chapter 11 (experiments and quasi-experiments), recalled, not read: the kindergarten differences estimates regress the student's total of the math and reading scaled scores on the class-type indicators (classk: small class, regular with aide), adding teacher experience (totexpk), school indicator variables, and sex, free-lunch eligibility and race. Schools enter as fixed effects, so the school is rendered as a random intercept and published_model is no. RULE GAP: the book's response is the sum tmathssk + treadssk, which is no column; the two scores are filed as two rows, each ignoring the other.
call: Stock and Watson's response is the sum of the math and reading scores, tmathssk + treadssk, which no column holds. The reading files each score as a row of its own (model 2 is treadssk), each ignoring the other. Is a response computed from two columns a response of this table, and if so, should the rows model the sum or each score?

formula: (1 - 3 / (4 * (exp_n + con_n) - 9)) * (exp_mean - con_mean) / sqrt(((exp_n - 1) * exp_n * exp_se^2 + (con_n - 1) * con_n * con_se^2) / (exp_n + con_n - 2)) ~ 1 + (1 | study_ID) + (1 | comp_ID)
notes: RULE GAP: no column holds the effect size. Help page dat.besson2016, examples: dat$sd_c <- con_se * sqrt(con_n); dat$sd_e <- exp_se * sqrt(exp_n); escalc(measure='SMD', m1i=exp_mean, m2i=con_mean, sd1i=sd_e, sd2i=sd_c, n1i=exp_n, n2i=con_n); mod1 <- rma.mv(yi ~ 1, V = vi, random = list(~ 1 | study_ID, ~ 1 | comp_ID)). The response names escalc's first input (the experimental group's mean), the formula's left side is the standardized mean difference (Hedges' g, its correction factor approximated) as an expression of the columns, and response_type is the effect size's; confidence is medium for that reason only. 473 comparisons of offspring behaviour (anxiety, exploration, activity) after maternal diet manipulation in rodents, from 55 studies (study_ID); comp_ID is unique per row, so its term is effect-level. dam_ID and animal_ID index dam and offspring groups the model does not fit, con_ID shared controls. The source weights each effect by its sampling variance, which the formula leaves out. Besson et al. (2016).
call: No column holds the effect size: the page computes a standardized mean difference with metafor's escalc from the arms' means, standard errors and sizes before fitting rma.mv with study_ID and comp_ID. The reading names exp_mean, escalc's first input, as the response and writes the effect size as the formula's left side. Is the computed effect size a response of this table, so that the row stands, or is the table `response missing or undocumented`?

formula: log((waward / (wtotal - waward)) / (maward / (mtotal - maward))) ~ type + (1 | study) + (1 | study:obs)
notes: RULE GAP: no column holds the effect size. Help page dat.bornmann2007, examples: escalc(measure='OR', ai=waward, n1i=wtotal, ci=maward, n2i=mtotal); res <- rma.mv(yi, vi, random = ~ 1 | study/obs) and, filed here, rma.mv(yi, vi, mods = ~ type, random = ~ 1 | study/obs) (fellowship vs grant applications). The response names escalc's first input (women awarded), the formula's left side is the log odds ratio of an award for women vs men as an expression of the columns (escalc adds 1/2 only to tables with a zero cell), and response_type is the effect size's; confidence is medium for that reason only. 66 award comparisons from 21 studies; obs numbers them within study, so study:obs has one level per row and its term is effect-level. The source weights each effect by its sampling variance, which the formula leaves out. Bornmann, Mutz & Daniel (2007), Journal of Informetrics.
call: No column holds the effect size: the page computes the log odds ratio of an award with metafor's escalc from the awarded and total applications of women and men before fitting rma.mv with study/obs. The reading names waward, escalc's first input, as the response and writes the effect size as the formula's left side. Is the computed effect size a response of this table, so that the row stands, or is the table `response missing or undocumented`?

notes: RULE GAP: no column holds the effect size. formula: (1 - 3 / (4 * (nt + nc) - 9)) * (mt - mc) / sqrt(((nt - 1) * sdt^2 + (nc - 1) * sdc^2) / (nt + nc - 2)) ~ 0 + outcome + (1 | study)
notes: RULE GAP: no column holds the effect size, and the long table mixes continuous outcomes (rnic1, rnic2, snic1, snic2: means and SDs) with binary ones (rngoal1, rngoal2, sngoal1, sngoal2: xt and xc of nt and nc). Help page dat.dagostino1998, examples: escalc SMD from mt, mc, sdt, sdc, nt, nc and escalc OR from xt, xc, nt, nc; rma(yi, vi) per outcome (one row per study each); V <- vcalc(vi, cluster=study, obs=esid, rho=0.7) and rma.mv(yi, V, mods = ~ 0 + outcome, subset=outcome %in% c('rnic1','rnic2')) with no random effects (no noteworthy heterogeneity), so published_model is no. The filed row is the reader's: the standardized mean difference (Hedges' g, correction approximated; the response names its first input mt) per continuous outcome with a study intercept, the binary outcomes' rows leaving it missing. 72 rows, 8 outcomes per antihistamine trial (9 studies). The source weights each effect by its sampling (co)variance, which the formula leaves out. D'Agostino et al. (1998).
call: No column holds the effect size: the page computes standardized mean differences for four continuous outcomes and log odds ratios for four binary ones with metafor's escalc from the arms' means, SDs, counts and sizes before fitting one rma per outcome. The reading names mt, escalc's first input, as the response and writes the effect size as the formula's left side. notes: RULE GAP: an arm-based network meta-analysis table whose page fits only netmeta. The book regresses testscr on the student-teacher ratio, adding the percent of English learners, the percent eligible for reduced-price lunch and the percent qualifying for CalWORKs (recalled from the cited book, not read), treating districts as independent. county repeats across districts, rendered as (1 | county) by the repeating-cluster ruling at low. distcod and district identify the row.

formula: log(packpc) ~ log(avgprs / cpi) + log(income / (pop * cpi)) + (1 | state)
notes: Read the Ecdat page: packs per capita of US states 1985-1995 with CPI, population, state personal income, taxes and the average price including sales taxes, referenced to Stock and Watson (2003, ch. 10). The book's instrumental-variables chapter regresses log packs on log real price, instrumented by the general sales tax (taxs - tax) and the cigarette-specific tax, with log real per capita income, on the 1995 cross-section and on the 1985-1995 differences (recalled, not read); no mixed model. The panel unit state is rendered as a random intercept by the panel ruling; the instruments tax and taxs are left out of the formula.

formula: log(crmrte) ~ log(prbarr) + log(polpc) + log(prbconv) + log(prbpris) + log(avgsen) + log(density) + log(wcon) + log(wtuc) + log(wtrd) + log(wfir) + log(wser) + log(wmfg) + log(wfed) + log(wsta) + log(wloc) + log(pctymle) + log(pctmin) + region + smsa + factor(year) + (1 | county)
notes: Read the Ecdat page: North Carolina counties 1981-1987 (Cornwell and Trumbull 1994; Baltagi 2006), referenced to Baltagi (2003) and linking plm's Crime, the same panel with the logarithms precomputed. plm's vignette (A_plmPackage.Rmd, Instrumental variable estimators, in the pinned plm 2.6-7) fits plm(lcrmrte ~ lprbarr + lpolpc + lprbconv + lprbpris + lavgsen + ldensity + lwcon + lwtuc + lwtrd + lwfir + lwser + lwmfg + lwfed + lwsta + lwloc + lpctymle + lpctmin + region + smsa + factor(year) | . - lprbarr - lpolpc + ltaxpc + lmix, data = Crime, model = "random"), the random-effects 2SLS of Baltagi (2005, p. 120, table 7.3), written here on this table's raw columns. The instruments taxpc and mix for prbarr and polpc are left out, so the formula is the random-effects model without instrumenting; medium for that departure.

formula: mrall ~ beertax + mlda + jaild + comserd + vmiles + unrate + log(perinc) + factor(year) + (1 | state)
notes: Read the Ecdat page: traffic fatality rate (deaths per 10000) of US states 1982-1988 (Ruhm) with the beer tax, minimum legal drinking age, mandatory jail and community service, miles per driver, unemployment rate and per capita income, referenced to Stock and Watson (2003, ch. 8). The book's panel chapter regresses the fatality rate on the beer tax with state, then state and time fixed effects, adding the drinking-age, punishment and economic controls with log real income (recalled, not read); only fixed-effects fits, so the panel unit state is rendered as a random intercept by the panel ruling and the time effects stay as factor(year). The book codes the drinking age as dummies; mlda enters as the age.

RESPONSE INFERRED: Read the Ecdat page: breach reports to the US Department of Health and Human Services of 500 or more compromised records, downloaded 2015-02-26, each with the covered entity, its type, the state where the breach occurred, the records compromised, the breach types and the locations of the information; the examples compute mean(Individuals.Affected) and tabulate breach types and locations, no model. Individuals.Affected (500 or more by law) taken as the response, breaches nested in State, an area factor with many levels, at low. Type.of.Breach and Location.of.Breached.Information combine several categories each and stay as columns outside the formula. Business.Associate.Present is derived from Covered.Entity.Type; Name.of.Covered.Entity and Web.Description are names and narrative text.

formula: log(oclc) ~ log(libprice / citestot) + I(log(libprice / citestot)^2) + I(log(libprice / citestot)^3) + log(2000 - date1) + log(2000 - date1):log(libprice / citestot) + log(charpp * pages / 1e6) + (1 | pub)
notes: Read the Ecdat page: economics journals in 2000 (Bergstrom) with publisher, library price, pages, characters per page, citations, founding year and library subscriptions (oclc), referenced to Stock and Watson (2003, ch. 6). The book's nonlinear-regression chapter regresses log subscriptions on log price per citation, its square and cube, log age, its interaction with log price per citation and log characters (recalled, not read), by OLS on journals as independent; the interaction of derived terms stays in the formula only. pub repeats across journals, rendered as (1 | pub) by the repeating-cluster ruling at low. oclc is a count the book models in logs, so family gaussian. title is the journal name; society and field are unused.

Read the Ecdat page: PSID individuals in 1993 with the 1968 interview number and person number, age, highest grade completed, labor income, annual hours, births and marital status, referenced to Cameron and Trivedi (2005, pp. 295-300). The book's program mma09p1np.do (cameron.econ.ucdavis.edu/mmabook) reads this file as females aged 30 to 50, codes educatn 0, 98 and 99 missing, drops zero earnings, top-codes earnings at 100000, keeps age == 36 and fits lowess and kernel regressions of ln(earnings/hours) on educatn; no parametric model. intnum identifies the 1968 family, which several women share, rendered as (1 | intnum) by the repeating-cluster ruling at low; most families hold one woman. The subset stays in these notes; persnum is the person number within the family; kids and married are unused.

formula: treadssk ~ classk + totexpk + sex + freelunk + race + (1 | schidkn)
notes: As row 1 with the reading scaled score; tmathssk ignored. Stock and Watson (2003) chapter 11, recalled: the response there is the total of both scores, with school indicators as fixed effects.

formula: I(choice == "choice1") ~ 0 + I(price1 - price2) + I(time1 - time2) + I(change1 - change2) + I(comfort1 - comfort2) + (0 + I(time1 - time2) + I(change1 - change2) + I(comfort1 - comfort2) | id)
notes: mlogit's vignette c5.mxl.qmd (read, cran/mlogit) fits mixed logits on mlogit's copy of this table (the same 2929 stated-preference choices of Meijer and Rouwendal, the attributes named price_A to comfort_B there): Train.mxlu <- mlogit(choice ~ price + time + change + comfort | - 1, Tr, panel = TRUE, rpar = c(time = "n", change = "n", comfort = "n"), R = 100, correlation = FALSE, halton = NA, method = "bhhh"), then Train.mxlc <- update(Train.mxlu, correlation = TRUE): correlated normal coefficients on time, change and comfort per individual (id), a fixed price coefficient and no alternative intercept (price rescaled to euros and time to hours there). With two alternatives the conditional logit is a logit of choosing choice1 on the attribute differences, so the formula renders the correlated model on I(x1 - x2). Meijer and Rouwendal (2006), cited by the help page, fit random-coefficient logits to these data. RULE GAP: the differences are no columns, so covariates list the eight attribute columns and random_slopes stays blank. choiceid numbers an individual's choice tasks, ignored.

formula: Tuna.choice ~ brand intercepts + price.<brand> (conditional logit, one price coefficient across the five brands) + household random brand intercepts and price slope by Tuna.hid
notes: Kim, Blattberg and Rossi (1995), JBES 13(3), 291-303, cited by the help page, abstract read on IDEAS/RePEc: a random-coefficient logit in which brand-specific intercepts and price-slope coefficients vary across households, fitted to household panel data of two product categories, its parametric heterogeneity distribution checked against semiparametric density estimates. Tuna.hid the household, Tuna.id its purchase occasions (ignored), Tuna.choice the brand chosen among five (Starkist and Chicken of the Sea in water and oil, store label in water), price.<brand> each brand's price at the purchase. RULE GAP: a multinomial (conditional) logit is outside Family, so family is blank, and the price slope sits on the alternatives' prices, which no one column holds. The paper's full specification was not read, hence medium.

formula: lnexp12m ~ lntotal + age + sex + hhsize + farm + educyr + (1 | commune)
notes: The help page cites Cameron and Trivedi (2005) pp. 88-90, the quantile regression of lnmed on lntotal in mma04p2qreg.do (qreg0902.dta: sex, age, educyr98, farm, urban98, hhsize, lhhexp1, lhhex12m, lnrlfood), with no commune term. The same book's section 24.7, pp. 848-53, Table 24.4, program mma24p1olscluster.do (read), takes the 5999 households of vietnam_ex1.dta in 194 communes and fits xtreg LNEXP12M LNHHEXP AGE SEX HHSIZE FARM EDUC, re and , mle after iis COMMUNE (random commune intercepts), beside OLS with cluster-robust errors and commune fixed effects. LNEXP12M is lnexp12m (lhhex12m) and LNHHEXP lntotal (lhhexp1); EDUC there is comped98 (completed diploma), which this table lacks, so educyr (years of schooling) stands in, hence medium. lnmed repeats lhhex12m under the quantile regression's name, ignored; urban and lnrlfood are not in the model.

RESPONSE INFERRED: breaches of health records of 500 or more people reported to HHS by June 2014; the help page fits no model (its examples take quantiles of Individuals_Affected and of the breach lengths). Individuals_Affected (records compromised per breach, at least 500 by law, heavy-tailed) is the outcome a reader would model, log-transformed with a gaussian family; State (the 50 states, DC and Puerto Rico) groups the breaches, a reader's choice; the breach type, the location of the breached information (multi-valued text categories) and year as covariates. Ignored: Number (record id), Name_of_Covered_Entity (the entity's name), Business_Associate_Involved, Summary, Date_of_Breach with its recodes breach_start and breach_end, and Date_Posted_or_Updated.

one annual series of US Postal Service income, expenses, post offices and mail volumes, 1789-2020

formula: log(fare) ~ concen + ldist + I(ldist^2) + y98 + y99 + y00 + (1 | id)
notes: Help page (Notes): "This data set nicely illustrates the different estimates obtained when applying pooled OLS, random effects, and fixed effects." Used in Text pages 506-507 and 581. Wooldridge, Introductory Econometrics, Ch. 14 computer exercise on AIRFARE (recalled, not read): log(fare) on year intercepts, concen, log(dist) and its square plus a route effect, estimated by pooled OLS, random effects and fixed effects; the row renders the random-effects fit with a random intercept on the route (id). Wooldridge's 2020 UK Stata Conference slides (Correlated Random Effects Methods for Panel Data, Sec. 4) fit the same panel by xtreg lfare concen y98 y99 y00, fe vce(cluster id) and by the Mundlak regression adding concenbar, ldist and the squared demeaned ldist. concen equals bmktshr (an alias, ignored), ldistsq is ldist^2 (written I(ldist^2)), lfare and lpassen are logs, and year is coded by y98, y99 and y00. Medium: the random-effects specification is recalled from the book.

formula: ecolbs ~ ecoprc + regprc + faminc + hhsize + educ + age + (1 | state)
notes: Help page (Notes): the price pairs "were randomly determined" and "the main dependent variable, ecolbs, piles up at zero, estimating a linear model is still worthwhile"; the demand equation regresses ecolbs on both prices (Used in Text pages 201, 223, 266, 626-627; the faminc, hhsize, educ and age controls are recalled from Wooldridge's exercises, not read). The source fits OLS without grouping. Respondents of the telephone survey repeat within their home state (state, a two-letter code), rendered as a random intercept at low, as a cluster the source treats as independent (HISTORY, Reading rulings). reglbs is the quantity of regular apples, an alternate response; id is the respondent.

formula: log(apps) ~ d93 + bowl + btitle + finfour + avg500 + stufac + top25 + (1 | school)
notes: RESPONSE INFERRED: the page names no model. Universities (school) observed in 1992 and 1993 (d93); "The 'athletic success' variables are for the year prior to the enrollment and academic data", and the table carries first differences of lapps, bowl, btitle, finfour, avg500, stufac and top25 (the c-prefixed columns), so the term project (Used in Text page 697, Ch. 19) relates the change in log applications to athletic success and academic quality. Rendered in levels with a random intercept on the university, Gaussian on log(apps). avg500 is (ver500 + mth500)/2, so its parts are ignored; bball is btitle or finfour; lapps_1 is the lag.

formula: log(avgsal) ~ bs + lenroll + lstaff + lunch + bsbar + lenrollbar + lstaffbar + lunchbar + (1 | distid)
notes: The page holds only the columns (no description, not marked as used in the text). They are elem94_95's Michigan elementary schools (schid, one row each) within districts (distid), whose page says the data "can be used to study the salary-benefits tradeoff, as in Chapter 4": log(avgsal) on the benefits-salary ratio bs with lenroll, lstaff and lunch (recalled from Wooldridge's Ch. 4 and 9 exercises). This table adds the within-district averages bsbar, lunchbar, lenrollbar and lstaffbar, the terms of Wooldridge's correlated random effects (Mundlak) approach for a cluster sample (Ch. 14, recalled, not read), so the formula carries them beside a random district intercept. bs is avgben/avgsal, so avgben is ignored; enroll and staff are the raw columns of the logged covariates.

formula: log(salary) ~ pubindx + top20phd + female + exper + I(exper^2) + assoc + prof + chair + factor(year) + (1 | id)
notes: Help page (Notes): "an unbalanced panel data set in the sense that as many as three years of data are available for each faculty member"; FE or FD would control away productivity, so "Pooled OLS regression with 'cluster robust' standard errors seems more natural", to measure "the effect of productivity on salary" and "the return to having a degree from a top 20 Ph.D. program" (Baser and Pema 2003; not used in the text). Pooled OLS only, so the faculty member (id) is a random intercept (Panels ruling). The terms are proposed from the page: publication index, top-20 Ph.D., sex, experience and its square, rank (assistant the reference), chair and year; the university dummies (osu to illinois) stay out of the formula. lsalary, expersq, the year dummies and pubindx's square, zero indicator and log are derived.

formula: lweekinc ~ educ + exper + I(exper^2) + (1 | state) + (1 | state:puma)
notes: RESPONSE INFERRED: the page lists the columns only (Census 2000 microdata provided by Abadie; Used in Text pages 452-453, Ch. 13, not read). The evident model is a log earnings equation in schooling and experience (expersq is exper^2, written I(exper^2)). Workers repeat within Public Use Microdata Areas inside states; puma codes repeat across states (100 in South Carolina, Nevada and Montana), so the area term is state:puma, nested in state. Grouping inferred from the columns, low.

Second response of the Battese, Harter and Fuller (1988) data over the same county grouping; see model 1. BHF predict the county areas of both crops from both pixel counts with a random county effect, as the registry's rabe_hesketh cropareas.dta row 2 records from its hand check; not read in the paper here, so medium.

formula: murdrate ~ execs + percblack + percmale + perc1019 + perc2029 + factor(year) + (1 | countyid)
notes: Help page: county panel 1980-1996 of murders, murder arrests and executions with county demographics (countyid "1000*statefips + countyfips"; Used in Text pages 16, 58, 431, 457). Wooldridge's exercises on COUNTYMURDERS (recalled, not read) relate the murder rate to executions by pooled OLS, first differences and fixed effects, with year effects, the demographic shares and a lag of execs that no column holds. FE and FD only, so the county is a random intercept (Panels ruling). murders is the count behind murdrate; arrests, arrestrate and execrate are alternate measures; lpopul is log(popul); statefips and countyfips make up countyid.

Help page: "These data are for the years 1972 and 1978 for 53 police districts in Norway" (Eide 1994, Tables A3 and A6). Wooldridge (Used in Text pages 464-465, recalled, not read) fits the distributed lag of log crime on the clear-up percentages of the prior year and of two years before by first differencing, the change in log(crime) on the changes in clrprc1 and clrprc2, and an exercise (pages 477-478) uses their average avgclr. FD only, so the district is a random intercept (Panels ruling); d78 carries the period intercept and codes year. The c-prefixed columns are the first differences.

formula: log(crmrte) ~ factor(year) + lprbarr + lprbconv + lprbpris + lavgsen + lpolpc + (1 | county)
notes: Wooldridge Example 13.9 (Used in Text pages 471-472) as Heiss, Using R for Introductory Econometrics (2nd ed.), Script 13.7 reproduces it: plm(log(crmrte) ~ d83+d84+d85+d86+d87+lprbarr+lprbconv+lprbpris+lavgsen+lpolpc, data = crime4.p, model = "fd") with pdata.frame(crime4, index = c("county","year")); Script 14.9 repeats it with cluster-robust standard errors. First differences only, so the county is a random intercept (Panels ruling) and the year dummies are factor(year). Cornwell and Trumbull (1994) North Carolina panel, a copy of rabe_hesketh crime.dta. The raw columns of the logged covariates, the other logs and the c-prefixed first differences are ignored.

Fast-food restaurants in New Jersey and Pennsylvania (Graddy 1997), one row each. Help page (Notes): "There are many possible dependent variables, namely, prices of various fast-food items. The key variable is the fraction of the population that is black, along with controls for poverty, income, housing values"; Wooldridge's Ch. 4 exercise (page 166, recalled, not read) regresses log(psoda) on prpblck, log(income) and prppov by OLS. Restaurants repeat within counties (county, "county label"), rendered as a random intercept at low; the zipcode variables repeat within zip codes, which have no column. RULE GAP: the table is also wide, the second wave's prices, wage, staff and hours as the columns ending in 2 (ignored as alternate responses), so its long form would add the restaurant as a grouping factor; it is filed for its county here, not as wide. NJ codes state and BK, KFC and RR code chain; pfries and pentree are alternate responses.

formula: totfatrte ~ bac08 + bac10 + perse + sbprim + sbsecon + sl70plus + gdl + perc14_24 + unem + vehicmilespc + factor(year) + (1 | state)
notes: Help page: the 48 continental states (state, alphabetical) 1980-2004 (Freeman 2007, "Drunk Driving Legislation and Traffic Fatalities: New Evidence on BAC 08 Laws"); Used in Text: "not used, but see page 695". Wooldridge's Ch. 13 and 14 exercises on DRIVING (recalled, not read) regress totfatrte on year dummies, bac08, bac10, perse, sbprim, sbsecon, sl70plus, gdl, perc14_24, unem and vehicmilespc by pooled OLS, first differences and fixed effects. FE and FD only, so the state is a random intercept (Panels ruling). The other fatality counts and rates are alternate responses; seatbelt is coded by sbprim and sbsecon, sl70, sl75 and slnone are summed into sl70plus, and d80 to d04 code year.

Indiana cities 1980-1988 with and without an enterprise zone (Papke 1994, the source of ezanders). Wooldridge Example 13.8 (Used in Text page 470, recalled, not read): log(uclms) on year effects and ez with a city effect, estimated by first differences; the exercise on page 504 uses fixed effects. FD and FE only, so the city is a random intercept (Panels ruling), Gaussian on the log of the claims count. c1 to c22 are the city dummies, d81 to d88 code year, and luclms, guclms and cez are the log, its change and the change in ez.

formula: trmgpa ~ spring + sat + hsperc + female + black + white + frstsem + tothrs + crsgpa + season + (1 | id)
notes: Students (id, "student identifier") of GPA2's university over the fall and spring terms (term, spring). The examples on pages 246-248 fit cumgpa on the spring term alone (Heiss, Using R for Introductory Econometrics, Script 7.7: lm(cumgpa ~ female*(sat+hsperc+tothrs), data = gpa3, subset = (spring==1))), with no repeated student. The Ch. 13 exercise on page 478 (recalled, not read) treats the student-athletes' two terms as a panel and asks whether athletes do worse in the term their sport is in season: trmgpa on spring, sat, hsperc, female, black, white, frstsem, tothrs, crsgpa and season by pooled OLS and first differences. Pooled OLS and FD only, so the student is a random intercept (Panels ruling). cumgpa is an alternate response, the c-prefixed columns are first differences, and term is coded by spring.

formula: log(scrap) ~ d88 + d89 + grant + grant_1 + (1 | fcode)
notes: Michigan manufacturing firms (fcode, "firm code number") 1987-1989 (Holzer et al. 1993). Wooldridge Example 14.1 (Used in Text pages 486-487, recalled, not read): fixed effects of log(scrap) on d88, d89, grant and the lagged grant grant_1; earlier examples difference 1987 and 1988, and Example 15.10 (Heiss, Using R for Introductory Econometrics, Script 15.6) fits plm(log(scrap) ~ hrsemp | grant, model = "fd", data = jtrain.p) with pdata.frame(index = c("fcode","year")). FE and FD only, so the firm is a random intercept (Panels ruling). rework is an alternate response; year is coded by d88 and d89; the logs of other columns and the c-prefixed first differences are derived.

formula: lowbrth ~ d90 + afdcprc + I(afdcprc^2) + lphypc + lbedspc + lpcinc + lpopul + (1 | state)
notes: Not used in the text of the help's edition; its notes say that afdcprc and its square give interesting findings for pooled OLS and fixed effects (first differencing) on these two years (1987, 1990) of 50 states. The other regressors are recalled from a later-edition computer exercise (lowbrth on d90, afdcprc, lphypc, lbedspc, lpcinc and lpopul by pooled OLS, then first differences), not checked; rendered per this pass's panel ruling with a state random intercept. infmort is the alternate response; stateabb aliases state and year aliases d90; the c* columns are first differences and afdcpsq the square; pcinc, physicpc, bedspc and popul are the raw forms of the logged regressors.

formula: math4 ~ lrexpp + lrexpp_1 + lenrol + lunch + factor(year) + (1 | distid)
notes: Wooldridge pages 479-480 and 505-506 use these Michigan district panels (Papke) in computer exercises; recalled, not checked: math4 on year dummies, log real spending per pupil and its lag, log enrollment and lunch, by first differences and fixed effects, no random-effects fit. Rendered per this pass's panel ruling with a district random intercept (550 districts, 1992-1998; 1992 has no lagged spending). intid, the intermediate school district that nests the districts, is not fitted. math7, drop and grad are alternate outcomes; the y* dummies code year; the other l*, g*, c*, *_1, *sq and *92 columns are transforms of spending, the foundation grant, enrollment, lunch and math4.

The help's notes: a simple regression of math4 on lexppp gives a negative coefficient and controlling for lunch makes the spending coefficient positive (Wooldridge page 18), OLS on Michigan elementary schools (bcode, one row each) in 2001. Schools repeat within districts (dcode), rendered as a district random intercept per the repeating-cluster ruling though the source treats schools as independent. read4 is the alternate response; expend, exppp and lexpend are other forms of spending; lenroll is log(enroll), which is unused.

Wooldridge (6th edition) pages 100, 145-146 and 198 use these 229 Michigan schools in computer exercises; recalled, not checked: math4 on pctsgle (percent of children in the school's zipcode not in married-couple families), then adding lmedinc and free, by OLS. Schools repeat within districts (dcode), rendered as a district random intercept per the repeating-cluster ruling; zipcode, the unit of the census columns (medinc, totchild, married, single, pctsgle), also repeats and is left out. read4 is the alternate response; lunch is free + reduced; lenroll and lexppp are logs of enroll and exppp.

Wooldridge pages 480, 505 and 548 use this state panel (1987, 1990, 1993) in computer exercises; recalled, not checked: mrdrte on year dummies, exec and unem by pooled OLS and first differences, then fixed effects and an IV version, no random-effects fit; rendered per this pass's panel ruling with a state random intercept on id. state is the postal code of id; d90 and d93 code year; the c* columns are first differences and their lags.

Not used in the text; the help's notes ask whether the preseason RPI helps predict performance (such as win percentage or making the NCAA tournament) once the previous year's post-season RPI is controlled for, by multiple regression, with probit or logit for the tournament indicator (row 2), and say coaching experience can be added. Teams repeat over seasons, rendered as a team random intercept per this pass's panel ruling. wins and losses give winperc; postrpi is this season's post-season rank, an outcome; conference, power5, recruitrank, postrpi_2 and coachexper are unused; year is the season.
Row 1's reading with the tournament indicator as response; the help's notes name probit or logit for it, so the logit of the contract's rule stands.

formula: pctstck ~ choice + prftshr + female + age + educ + finc25 + finc35 + finc50 + finc75 + finc100 + finc101 + wealth89 + stckin89 + irain89 + (1 | id)
notes: Wooldridge page 506 (a chapter 14 computer exercise, recalled, not checked): some rows are spouses of one family (id), a cluster sample with clusters of at most two; pctstck is regressed by OLS on these regressors ignoring the clustering, then with cluster-robust errors and family fixed effects (Papke 2004, National Longitudinal Survey of Mature Women). Rendered per this pass's panel ruling with a family random intercept. pctstck holds three ordered codes (0 mostly bonds, 50 mixed, 100 mostly stocks) fitted as linear, hence gaussian. pyears, married and black are unused.

formula: lcriv ~ lpris + log(polpc) + log(incpc) + unem + black + metro + ag0_14 + ag15_17 + ag18_24 + ag25_34 + factor(year) + (1 | state)
notes: Wooldridge pages 573-574 (a chapter 16 computer exercise after Levitt 1996, recalled, not checked): the change in log violent crime gcriv on gpris and the changes of the controls (gpolpc, gincpc, cunem, cblack, cmetro, the age shares) with year dummies, by OLS on the first differences and then with final1 and final2 instrumenting gpris; no random-effects fit. The source weights each effect by its sampling variance (from n and items), which the formula leaves out. Demir et al. (2022), a reliability generalization meta-analysis.

The source fits the percentage as a normal outcome weighted by its sampling variance, which the formula leaves out. Further fits on the page: random = ~ bmicent | study with struct='GEN' (a random slope on the same grouping, not a row) and a restricted cubic spline rcs(bmicent, 4). bmi is the interval midpoint, bmi.lb and bmi.ub its bounds; ch, dm and mg are study-level exclusion criteria. Help page fits two univariate rma(yi, sei=sei, method='DL') on the DFS and the OS rows. The cited source Riley et al. (2007, Stat Med 26:78-97; erratum Riley 2011) fits a bivariate random-effects meta-analysis of the two log hazard ratios with correlated study effects per outcome (abstract read: BRMA compared with univariate fits on two examples), in metafor terms rma.mv(yi, vi, mods = ~ 0 + outcome, random = ~ outcome | study, struct='UN'), written as (outcome | study). 81 studies, 17 with both outcomes. vi is the sampling variance (sei its root), which the source weights by; the within-study correlation the bivariate model needs is not in the table. Model recalled from the cited paper, not fitted on the page.

Help page only plots the dose-toxicity curves per study (12 phase I studies of irinotecan and S-1, several doses each). Roever et al. (2022, Stat Med 41:3915-3940; abstract read) propose a two-stage approach: penalized logistic regression of dose-limiting toxicity on dose within each study, then a Bayesian random-effects meta-analysis of the per-study estimates. Its one-stage counterpart is the logistic GLMM written here with study random intercepts and log-dose slopes (the log-dose scale recalled, not read); the two-stage fit is not a mixed model on this table, so published_model no. Ursino et al. (2021) fit a one-stage hierarchical model to the sorafenib twin dat.ursino2021.

formula: cbind(deaths, n - deaths) ~ factor(study) + group + (0 + group | study)
notes: Help page example: pairwise(treat = group, event = deaths, n = n, studlab = study, sm = 'OR'), then metabin with method = 'glmm', model = 'CM.AL', random = TRUE, a random-effects conditional logistic GLMM (metafor's rma.glmm with the approximate hypergeometric likelihood), beside IV, Mantel-Haenszel, Peto and penalized logistic fits (Tian et al. 2009, Biostatistics). Conditioning on each trial's total events stands for fixed study effects, with a random treatment effect per study: written as factor(study) + group + (0 + group | study), filed as an uncorrelated slope. 48 two-arm trials of rosiglitazone vs control; the six double-zero trials it adds are what separates it from dat.nissen2007. infarcts is the other outcome (Nissen and Wolski's primary), not modelled on the page; n.all counts all patients, n those with outcome data. intervention and detailed.intervention name the arm's drugs.

Help page only plots the dose-toxicity curves per study (13 phase I trials of sorafenib, several doses each). The cited source Ursino, Roever, Zohar and Friede (2021, Ann Appl Stat 15:174-193; abstract read) fits a Bayesian curve-free hierarchical model on the logistic scale to these trials: a toxicity probability per dose with study random effects that follow an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck Gaussian process over doses, priors from a latent Gamma process. Rendered as a dose factor with a study random intercept; the process over doses is not representable. Roever et al. (2022) fit a two-stage penalized logistic regression and random-effects meta-analysis to both datasets (see dat.roever2022). Model recalled from the cited paper, not fitted on the page; its priors are given in words only.

detail: dat.berkey1998 with the two rows of each trial in reverse order (AL first, v1i and v2i swapped accordingly), as the shared help page states.
20 hypothetical trials the page says were constructed to illustrate model checking (Viechtbauer 2021, Handbook of meta-analysis); also one row per trial, the arms as columns
one effect per study: nine Cronbach's alphas of the CES-D scale (ai with mi items and ni), rma on the ARAW, AHW and ABT measures with caregivers as moderator.
one row per study, the arms as columns: 19 trials of complementary and alternative medicine for irritable bowel syndrome, responders x.a of n.a vs x.p of n.p, escalc RR and rma (DL).

one row per study, the arms as columns: 136 comparisons from 133 nicotine replacement studies (a few test two NRT types), abstinent x.nrt of n.nrt vs x.ctrl of n.ctrl, rma.mh per treatment type and combined.

wide: one row per study and patient group (34 rows, 29 studies), true positives of cases (tp of np) and true negatives of non-cases (tn of nn) as columns; rma per patient group on diagnostic log odds ratios, and a bivariate rma.mv with random = ~ group | study on a stacked to.long copy of the asymptomatic subset.
one effect per study, the DAS-28 and HAQ mean differences as columns, each meta-analysed alone by metagen (common effect); no grouping beyond the study
one row per study, the arms as columns (2x2 counts non.pos, non.neg, cir.pos, cir.neg); rma on log odds ratios, also by category

notes: psymetadata documents the data only: 67 standardized mean differences of red vs a control color on test performance, study_id (22 per the page) and es_id one per row. Gnambs (2020, Psychon Bull Rev 27:1374-1382; PMC7704521, method read): the effect sizes were pooled using a random-effects model with REML in metafor, and because some studies provided more than one effect size, a multivariate meta-analysis was specified that acknowledged the sampling covariances (Gleser and Olkin); tau^2 is reported between the 38 independent samples, which have no column, so study_id (the publication holding them) stands in. Moderators were the control color, color matching, presentation and the cognitive measure. vi is the sampling variance, which the source weights by.

psymetadata documents the data only (OSF ux3eh): a subset of Many Labs 2 (Klein et al. 2018, Adv Methods Pract Psychol Sci), one effect per replicating lab (lab) and replicated finding (analysis), in r (yi_r, vi_r) and in d (yi_d, vi_d, the same effect on another scale). The paper meta-analyses each finding across samples (not read here), so rows repeat within lab across findings, crossed; lab is rendered as a random intercept and the finding as a covariate. Lab-level moderators: country, weird, western, educated, industrialized, rich, democratic, mean_weird_score, online. vi_r is the sampling variance, which the source weights by. RULE GAP: per-finding fits treat the labs as independent; the lab counted as a cluster, published_model no.

psymetadata documents the data only (OSF fq5wp): 2,443 Fisher-z effects from 131 meta-analyses of intelligence research, study_id indexing the meta-analysis, es_id the effect, es and se the effect on its original scale (type_es). Nuijten et al. (2020, J Intell 8:36; PMC7720125, method read): a two-step strategy, a random-effects meta-regression on the standard error within each meta-analysis with rma() in metafor (Paule-Mandel), then a random-effects meta-analysis of the per-meta-analysis coefficients; a multilevel model of primary studies nested in meta-analyses was tried but failed to converge (footnote 2). Proposed: the effects nested in meta-analyses. vi is the sampling variance, which the source weights by.

psymetadata documents the data only (PsyArXiv gjqcs): 99 Hedges' g effects of executive function in intellectual disability vs mental-age-matched controls from 26 studies (study_id), es_id one per row, group_id the aetiology (NSID, FXS, DS, WS), ef_type, ef_component, domain and test. Spaniol and Danielsson (2022, J Intellect Disabil Res 66:9-31; PubMed abstract): a multilevel random-effects meta-analysis, g = -0.34, aetiology a significant moderator; the levels were not read, rendered as effects nested in studies. vi is the sampling variance, which the source weights by.

psymetadata documents the data only (OSF szfwx): 76 correlations of learning goal orientation with performance adaptation from 35 studies (study_id), es_id one per row; stasielowicz2019b holds the performance goal orientation effects. Stasielowicz (2019, J Res Pers 82:103847; abstract via search): three-level meta-analyses were conducted for learning goal orientation and performance goal orientation, rendered as effects nested in studies. age_imputed fills age. vi is the sampling variance, which the source weights by; n enters it.

psymetadata documents the data only (OSF szfwx): 86 correlations of performance goal orientation with performance adaptation from 28 studies (study_id), es_id one per row, pgo_type the goal orientation (avoid, prove, global); stasielowicz2019a holds the learning goal orientation effects. Stasielowicz (2019, J Res Pers 82:103847; abstract via search): three-level meta-analyses for learning and performance goal orientation, rendered as effects nested in studies; whether pgo_type splits the fits was not read. age_imputed fills age. vi is the sampling variance, which the source weights by; n enters it.

detail: per-lab and age-group effect sizes (d_z with variance) aggregated from the ManyBabies 1 trial table, which this pass reads in Tier O; the paper fits rma(d_z ~ 1, vi = d_z_var) on them (mb1-analysis-public paper/mb1-paper.Rmd)

formula: rides ~ user + temp_actual + weekend + humidity + weather_cat + (1 | date)
notes: Help page: daily observations, 267 each for registered and casual riders, so each date holds two rows. Bayes Rules! Chapter 11 (chapter-11) plots rides against temp_actual, weekend, humidity and weather_cat by user and splits the table by user (filter(user == 'casual')), fitting no model on it. Proposed: a Poisson model of rides by user type and the day's weather, date the grouping factor of the paired rows (a column that indexes a unit the rows repeat within, #133). Days from the UCI Bike Sharing data (Fanaee-T and Gama 2013).

RESPONSE INFERRED: the help page documents late-December Ontario counts of each species per year (1921-2017), one row per species and year, with no model. Bayes Rules! fits Normal, Poisson and Negative Binomial regressions only on its one-species subsets (bald_eagles in Exercises 12.5-12.9, loons). Proposed: the count with the person-hours as exposure and a species intercept. species_latin aliases species; count_per_hour and count_per_week are the count over hours.

Bayes Rules! Exercise 16.2 (chapter-16, hierarchical models without predictors) asks whether farm_name and processing_method are grouping variables or predictors in a model of total_cup_points; batches repeat within farms, so farm_name groups. Exercise 17.14 (chapter-17) asks for a hierarchical model of total cup points over 'multiple batches from each of 27 farms' on coffee_ratings_small, a simplified version of this table excluded as derived, and leaves the predictors to the reader. Proposed: the one-way model of Chapter 16. total_cup_points sums the grades aroma to sweetness with clean_cup and a cupper score not in the table (CQI scoring), so the grades nearly determine it. species is row 2's response.

Bayes Rules! Exercise 18.1 (chapter-18) poses a hierarchical model of whether a batch is of the Robusta species by its flavor on coffee_ratings and leaves the grouping variable to the reader; farm_name is the grouping of row 1 (Exercises 16.2 and 17.14). total_cup_points is row 1's response.

Help page: one row per respondent of the popvssoda.com volunteer survey with the respondent's state and census region; pop marks the respondents whose word_for_cola is pop, so word_for_cola is ignored as the response's source. Bayes Rules! uses the table to illustrate Bayes' rule over regions and fits no model on it. Proposed: a logistic model with region and a state intercept; states nest in regions (an area factor with many levels groups, LGAclaims).

detail: The help page calls it a subset of the airbnb data (869 of the 1561 Chicago listings, the same columns); Bayes Rules! fits its models on airbnb (Sections 18.2 and 19.1).

One species' late-December Ontario counts (Bald Eagle, 1981-2017), one row per year; the help page points to bird_counts as the more complete table it comes from. Bayes Rules! Exercises 12.5-12.9 model count by year and hours without grouping.

A simplified version of coffee_ratings (help page): 636 of its batches with farm_name, total_cup_points and nine grades. Bayes Rules! Exercise 17.14 poses a hierarchical model of total cup points by farm on it and leaves the predictors to the reader; filed on coffee_ratings.
One species' late-December Ontario counts (loons, 2000-2017), one row per year; the help page points to bird_counts as the more complete table it comes from.
A random sample of 100 artists of the MoMA collection (help page), a subset of moma without department.

Two of weather_australia's three stations (help page: weather_australia combines this data with a third city); Bayes Rules! Chapter 11 fits temp3pm by temp9am and location, a two-level fixed predictor.

A random 1000 hotel bookings, one row each; hotel has two levels, and agent, company and country classify bookings. Bayes Rules! Exercises 13.6-13.9 model is_canceled by logistic regression without grouping.

notes: StroupGLMM Exam3.3 (Example 3.3, p. 77, 'RCBD data with fixed location effect') fits lm(Y ~ trt + loc), and Exam3.5 lm(Y ~ A + B + loc); a fixed-effects fit over blocks is rendered with random locations (mead.germination ruling).
The help page names S1 and S2 the two binomial responses over the Nbin subjects of each location and treatment; no example fits S1. Proposed: row 1's model.

formula: cbind(Fav, N - Fav) ~ X + (1 + X || Batch)
notes: Help page: Fav the successes of N independent Bernoulli trials per batch and time; no example fits them. Proposed as row 1.
The help page calls Count a binomial response variable but names no trials for it, so it is filed as a count; no example fits it. Proposed as row 1.

StroupGLMM Exam8.1 (Example 8.1, p. 250, nested factorial): lmer(y ~ set + trt %in% set + (1|set/block)), whose (1|set/block) expands to (1|set) + (1|set:block). The (1|set) term beside the fixed two-level set is aliased, so the row keeps the blocks-within-sets term (Cultivation ruling); set:block is block, since the ten blocks are numbered across sets. The six treatments nest in the two sets (help page), so trt %in% set codes as trt.

StroupGLMM Exam9.2 (Example 9.2, p. 276, two-way random effects nested model): the help page nests the levels of b within those of a, and the page's fixed version is lm(y ~ a + b %in% a), but its mixed fit lmer(y ~ (1|b/a)) nests a in b and then reads ranef(...)$a, which that fit lacks; filed as the intended (1|a/b) (an evident bug files the intended model, voorspoels).

StroupGLMM Exam9.4 (Example 9.4, p. 288, BLUP and fixed effect estimators): a and b as factors; lmer(y ~ a + (1|b) + (1|a/b)), whose (1|a/b) expands to (1|a) + (1|a:b). The (1|a) term beside the fixed two-level a is aliased, so the row keeps b and a:b (Cultivation ruling).

formula: cbind(Fav, N - Fav) ~ X + (1 + X || Batch)
notes: Help page: Fav the successes of N Bernoulli trials per batch and time; no example fits them. Proposed as row 1.

detail: Six rows, two per treatment; Exam2.B.3 fits lm(y ~ trt).
An unequal-slopes ANCOVA, one row per unit; Exam7.3 fits aov(y ~ trt*x) and lm(y ~ 0 + trt/x).

formula: eng ~ mot + gpa + grade + rural + frpm + (1 | school)
notes: Help page: student engagement of 528 students in 40 schools, school the clustering variable, rural and frpm school-level; example data for missing data (engage.miss deletes values from it). No model on the page or in the package; the title names engagement the outcome. Proposed: every documented predictor with a school intercept. Companion of Huang, Practical Multilevel Modeling Using R (Sage), whose code sits behind the publisher's login.

Help page: y the outcome, w1 a level-2 and x1 a level-1 predictor, group the cluster identifier of 30 groups; 'example data for testing the need for a random intercept', which 'illustrates the need to adjust the p values for a modified LRT'. No model call on the page.
Help page: as ri_test1, with 3,000 rows in 30 groups; 'LRT results show that a random slope is not warranted', so the random-intercept model stands. No model call on the page.

formula: sus ~ male + gpa + fight + pminor + (1 | school)
notes: Help page: 8465 students from 100 Virginia schools; sus the self-reported suspension, fight, male, gpa and the school's percent minority enrollment pminor. No model on the page; the title names suspension the outcome. Proposed: a logistic model with the documented predictors and a school intercept. ztc, frpmp and frpl are undocumented; the centered copies (gpa.c, pminor.c, frpm.c, frmp.c) and the school mean gpam are ignored as derived.

formula: pv1math ~ escs + othl + intmat + private + schsize + (1 | schoolid)
notes: RESPONSE INFERRED: help page: PISA students of Thailand in schools, 'example data to be used for centering', no model. thai.sm, its reduced version (excluded as derived), keeps math (the first plausible value in mathematics), escs, othl, intmat, private, schsize and schoolid, so the row takes those as the response and predictors. The reading plausible values are alternate responses and w_fstuwt the student weight.

detail: The author's data-raw/centerexample.R (github.com/flh3/MLMusingR) draws it: set.seed(123), y and x from rnorm for the first cluster, and anscombiser::mimic copies shifted by 2 and 4 for clusters 2 and 3. The help page calls it 60 observations from 3 clusters for discussing within and between group effects.
engage (the complete data) with values deleted for the missing-data example (help page: 'this has missing data'), the same rows and columns.
The help page points to the simulation code of the UCLA OARC page (stats.oarc.ucla.edu/r/codefragments/mesimulation) for its patients nested in doctors nested in hospitals.
A reduced version of thai (help page title 'Thai data from PISA (reduced)', usage data(thai)): 4271 of its rows, with math (thai's pv1math) and six of its columns.

formula: a_point ~ I(gcse_tot / gcse_no - 6) + I((gcse_tot / gcse_no - 6)^2) + gender + (1 + I(gcse_tot / gcse_no - 6) | lea:estab)
notes: Read the help page example: runMLwiN(logit(a_point, cons, 6) ~ 1 + gcseav[1:5] + I(gcseav^2)[1:5] + gender[1:5] + (1[1:5] + gcseav[1:5] | school), D = 'Ordered Multinomial', EstM = 1) with gcseav = gcse_tot/gcse_no - 6 and school the lea and estab combination (the page: establishment codes alone do not identify schools). [1:5] gives one coefficient across the five cumulative logits, a proportional-odds model, so the family is the rule's cumulative logit; MCMC with MLwiN's default priors. pupil is the pupil id and cons the constant. RULE GAP: the random slope is on gcseav, a ratio of two columns; filed as gcse_tot|lea:estab, the formula carries the ratio.

Read the help page example: after relevel(use4, 4), runMLwiN(log(use4, cons) ~ 1 + lc + (1 | district), D = 'Unordered Multinomial', EstM = 1, nonlinear = c(1, 2)), Not_using_contraception the reference category. RULE GAP: an unordered multinomial logit (brms categorical) is outside Family, so family is blank. use is the binary recoding of use4 (alternate response), woman the level-1 id and cons the constant. lc is an ordered factor (the page: ordered levels; the example notes ordered predictors are fitted with treatment contrasts). 2867 women in 61 districts, a larger subset of the 1989 Bangladesh Fertility Survey than bang1.

detail: The complete cases of gcsemv1 (title: complete cases only): 1523 of its 1905 pupils in the same 73 schools, without agemths. The help page fits the same bivariate model as gcsemv1, runMLwiN(c(written, csework) ~ 1 + female + (1 | school) + (1 | student), D = 'Multivariate Normal').
The page calls it a simulated dataset of office workers' salaries with multiple membership of companies (Browne 2012).

One row per Scottish region (56 regions, male lip cancer 1975-1980, Clayton and Kaldor 1987). The help page fits runMLwiN(log(obs) ~ 1 + perc_aff + offset(offs) + (0 | neigh1) + (1 | area), D = 'Poisson'), a multiple-membership CAR term over neigh1 to neigh11 beside a region-level heterogeneity term with one row per level; neither is a grouping factor.

formula: cbind(NumYes, NumNo) ~ factor(ContCntr) + I(1000 * TargCntr) + (0 + I(1000 * TargCntr) | Obs) + (1 + I(1000 * TargCntr) | Obs:ContCntr)
notes: Read MPDiR inst/scripts/Ch9.R (Knoblauch and Maloney 2012, ch. 9, mixed-effects models): with TrgCnt1000 = 1000 * TargCntr and FCtxCnt = factor(ContCntr), Context.glmm1 to Context.glmm3b compare random structures by anova and the final Context.glmm4 <- glmer(cbind(NumYes, NumNo) ~ FCtxCnt + TrgCnt1000 + (TrgCnt1000 + 0 | Obs) + (TrgCnt1000 | Obs:FCtxCnt), family = binomial('probit')). Six observers, four flanker contrasts, five target contrasts. RULE GAP: successes beside failures without a trials column are filed count (as faraway soybean), NumNo ignored; a binomial probit is outside Family, so family is blank; the by-observer term is a slope without an intercept, filed as TargCntr||Obs.

The help page names no model, only a lattice plot of Response against Contrast per Cell, and MPDiR's chapter scripts do not use the table. Six cells of macaque V1 and V2 at seven contrasts (Peirce 2007, on saturating contrast-response functions); Response is a mean firing rate over N trials with its SEM, an aggregate response on a real grouping, so low. Type and Area are cell-level columns. The linear form stands in for a contrast-response function.

Read MPDiR inst/scripts/Ch9.R (Knoblauch and Maloney 2012, ch. 9): clmm(factor(SimRating) ~ sibs + (1 | Obs), data = Faces, link = 'probit'), a cumulative probit with observer intercepts; chapter 3 fits the fixed clm and tests agediff and gendiff by addterm. Image (30 image pairs) is crossed with Obs (32 observers) and enters model 2. RULE GAP: SimRating is an 11-point rating (0 to 10), past the ordinal cap of ten levels, so it is filed count with family cumulative(probit).

formula: SimRating ~ sibs + (0 + sibs | Obs) + (0 + sibs | Image)
notes: Read MPDiR inst/scripts/Ch9.R: Faces.glmm <- polmer(SimRating ~ sibs + (sibs1 - 1 | Obs) + (sibs1 - 1 | Image), data = Faces, lnk = 'probit'); polmer, defined at the top of the script, expands the ratings into cumulative binary responses and fits glmer with a binomial probit, sibs1 the sibling indicator. RULE GAP: the random terms are slopes on sibs without intercepts, filed as sibs||Obs and sibs||Image; the 11-point response is filed count as in row 1.

Read MPDiR inst/scripts/Ch9.R: F2.glmm1 <- glmer(Resp ~ Stim + (1 | Obs) + (1 | Image), data = Faces2, family = binomial(probit)), crossed observers and image pairs read as a signal-detection model (d-prime and criterion); F2.glmm2 to F2.glmm4 add Stim slopes by Obs, Image or both and are compared by anova, the same grouping. RULE GAP: the first eight rows' Resp equal SimRating > 5 of the same observer and image pairs in Faces, so Faces2 may be Faces dichotomized; the page calls it a Yes/No judgment, and it is filed as its own table.

formula: cbind(round(N * p / 100), N - round(N * p / 100)) ~ log(Q) + (1 + log(Q) | Obs:Run)
notes: Read MPDiR inst/scripts/Ch1.R: after renaming Q and p to Quanta and PerCent, NumYes = round(N * PerCent/100) and id = interaction(Obs, Run), HSP1.glm <- glm(cbind(NumYes, NumNo) ~ id/log(Quanta) - 1, binomial(probit)) fits one probit psychometric function per observer and run, against HSP0.glm with one common function. The five functions (three observers, one of them with two runs; Hecht, Shlaer and Pirenne 1942) are rendered with random intercepts and log-quanta slopes at low, as a fixed-effects fit over blocks. p is a percentage, continuous with its denominator N in the formula. RULE GAP: a binomial probit is outside Family, so family is blank.

Read MPDiR inst/scripts/Ch2.R: lm(LnThresh ~ Mtype + Sex + LnAge), interactions tested by update(. ~ .^2) and Sex dropped (Motion.lm2), a pooled fit. 70 observers, some with both a first- and a second-order threshold (112 rows; Thibault et al. 2007), so Subject is a grouping factor the source does not fit, rendered as a random intercept at medium.

detail: The afex_plot vignette calls it synthetic data from Maxwell and Delaney (2004, p. 547), and the page hypothetical reaction-time data: ten subjects, six cells each.

notes: The page describes the design and fits no model: both soleus muscles of seven rats, one randomized to pinacidil and one to placebo, contraction force measured every 30 seconds on 15 occasions (Kristensen and Hansen 2004, a tutorial on repeated measures). Rendered with rat and muscle (rat:cond) intercepts and time as a factor. values are normalized to the first time point, so time 0 is 100 for every muscle.

The page describes a split-plot design and fits no model: six pregnant mice randomized to valproic acid or saline (group, constant within litter), their 24 offspring randomized to MPEP or saline (drug), two levels of randomization; a balanced subset of Mehta et al. (2011) via Lazic and Essioux (2013). Rendered with a litter intercept; sex is not in the design's model. activity is an integer locomotor activity count.

The page gives the design in one line and fits no model: cell counts per well of six 1536-well plates from a high-throughput screen. Rendered with a plate intercept; row and column are well positions on the plate (coordinates), ignored.

The page describes the nested design and fits no model: six rats randomized to three treatments (two each), each liver cut into three pieces, two measurements per piece; the rats are the experimental units with two levels of subsampling (Sokal and Rohlf 1995). Rats are numbered within treatment and pieces within rat, so the factors are Treatment:Rat and Treatment:Rat:Liver.

The page describes the design and fits no model: ten patients randomized to high or low dietary calcium (five each), blood pressure at three time points (Casella 2008). Rendered with a patient intercept and time as a factor.

The page describes the design and fits no model: 47 rats randomized to drug or saline, distance traveled in the open field per 15-minute interval over 90 minutes. Rendered with a rat intercept and time as a factor.

detail: The page calls it simulated data for two outcome variables (five samples with three technical replicates each).
The page calls it simulated data for an assay window between positive and negative control samples.
The page calls it simulated data contrasting blocking with covariate adjustment (eight rats, two designs).

notes: The page describes the design and its coding and fits no model: weekly engagement of 131 band members over 16 weeks, with TRANS and RECOV provided for a discontinuous growth model around an unexpected football win before the twelfth collection (Bliese and Lang 2016). Rendered as that growth model with a person intercept; the Big Five scores, FEMALE, TENURE and RET.15 are person-level columns not in it.

The page names the special issue's three scales but no model, and the package's tutorial uses the table only for rwg(j) agreement. The special issue (Bliese, Halverson and Schriesheim 2002) benchmarks HLM, WABA and random group resampling on whether leadership climate moderates the relation of a stressor to well-being, here task significance and hostility, among 2042 soldiers in 49 companies; rendered with a company intercept. The items LEAD01 to HOSTIL05 make up the scale scores and GLEAD, GTSIG and GHOSTILE are company means (derived), all ignored; SUB is the subject id.

formula: roani ~ time + trans + post + boardindprop + dirageavg + femaledirsprop + debtassets + lnemp + ceotenure + (1 | companyid)
notes: The page describes the panel and its coding and fits no model: 196 firms observed 2007 to 2011 (980 rows; the format says 960), time, trans and post coded for a discontinuous growth model at the 2009 recession, and yearly board-composition predictors, a panel for contrasting fixed-effect and mixed-effect models (Bliese et al. 2020). roani, return on assets, is the one outcome column. Rendered as the growth model plus the predictors with a firm intercept. companyname duplicates companyid and year equals time + 2007, both ignored.

detail: The page calls it a simulated data set created by Paul Bliese (Klein et al. 2000).

formula: Resp ~ Item1 + Item2 + Item3 + Item4 - 1 + (1 | ID)
notes: Help example Fitted.irt <- mixor(Resp ~ Item1 + Item2 + Item3 + Item4 - 1, data = irt.data, id = ID, weights = freq, which.random.slope = 1:4, link = "logit", nAGQ = 10, random.effect.mean = FALSE, UNID = 1), a two-parameter logistic IRT model of four ASVAB arithmetic reasoning items (Mislevy 1985). RULE GAP: the 2PL gives one subject effect an item-specific loading (random slopes on the four item indicators, unidimensional), which lme4 syntax cannot state; filed as its equal-loading (Rasch) form, a random intercept on ID. The four item indicators sum to one, as the source fits them without an intercept. Each ID is a response pattern by sex (32 patterns, four rows each) and freq its frequency weight (ignored, as twin_hay). Fitted.irt2 adds the SexItem1-4 products of sex and item on the same grouping, not a row; SexF stays a column.

formula: CD4 ~ obstime + obstime:drug + gender + prevOI + AZT + (obstime | id)
notes: aids.Rd and the joineR vignette describe the trial and fit nothing to aids. The page's source, Guo and Carlin (2004, The American Statistician 58:16-24), fits the CD4 trajectory separately (SAS PROC MIXED) and jointly with the time to death: time, time by drug, gender, previous opportunistic infection and the AZT stratum, with a random intercept and slope per patient; recalled from the paper's AIDS example, not read, so medium. CD4 holds the square-rooted count. RULE GAP: the source fits drug only through obstime:drug, but the row grammar needs drug among the covariates. time and death are the survival outcome.

mpjlcmm.Rd example 1 fits mult1 <- multlcmm(MMSE + BVRT ~ age65 + I(age65^2) + CEP + male, random = ~ age65 + I(age65^2), subject = "ID", link = c("5-quant-splines", "4-quant-splines"), data = paquid), age65 = (age - 65)/10, then joins it with the dementia time in mpjlcmm(). RULE GAP: MMSE and BVRT measure one latent process, each through an estimated quantile-spline link, which has no registry family; family blank and the formula states BVRT's marker alone, so medium. BVRT is an integer score 0-15, so count.

mpjlcmm.Rd example 2 fits mCESD1 <- lcmm(CESD ~ age65 + I(age65^2) + male, random = ~ age65 + I(age65^2), subject = "ID", link = "5-quant-splines", data = paquid), age65 = (age - 65)/10, a latent process mixed model then joined with MMSE and the dementia time in mpjlcmm(). RULE GAP: the estimated quantile-spline link has no registry family, so family is blank. CESD is an integer depression score 0-52, so count.

detail: help page: "The data were simulated from a 3-latent class linear mixed model"
help page: "The data were simulated from a joint latent class mixed model with 3 classes"
help page title "Simulated dataset simdataHADS": repeated HADS items simulated to mimic the PREDIALA study

notes: The help page lists Colourbalance among the 15 response variables and fits only Coloursaturation (model 1); that model on this response, the page's next in order, is proposed.
The help page lists Noise among the 15 response variables and fits only Coloursaturation (model 1); that model on this response, the page's next in order, is proposed.

epileptic.qol.Rd, the other help pages, the vignettes and the tests fit no model to this table. The page cites Jacoby et al. (2015, Epilepsia 56:460-472), whose abstract says the QoL data "were analyzed using longitudinal data models" and the continuous measures explored with joint models, with no specification I could read; the model is proposed: the score over time by arm with a patient intercept. Multivariate table: anxiety, depress and aep (the NEWQOL scores, higher worse), in the page's order, are models 1 to 3. The scores are integers (the help: continuous measures), so count, fitted Gaussian as linear joint models fit them. time is the day each questionnaire came back; with.time, with.status and with.status2 are the treatment-failure outcome.

Help page (shared with ant111b): the Antigua corn yield trials of Andrews and Herzberg (1985, pp. 339-353), site a factor with 8 levels, block I to IV within each site, plot within block, trt a factor of 12 treatments, harvwt 'the average yield'; ears codes missing values as -9999 and is an alternate response, id is a row id and plot the plot's position in its block (all ignored). No model on the page. Maindonald, Braun and Andrews (2024) Sections 7.1-7.2 (code ch7.qmd at github.com/jhmaindonald/Rcode) and DAAG 3rd ed. Subsection 10.1.3 (scripts/mlm.html) fit ant111b.lmer <- lmer(harvwt ~ 1 + (1 | site), data=ant111b) on ant111b, the block means of treatment 111 (excluded as derived). Help page: 'Each of 20 tasters each assessed three out of the four varieties. The experiment was conducted according to a balanced incomplete block design'; aftertaste is a mark on a scale from 0 (extreme dislike) to 150 (like very much). The help example and Maindonald, Braun and Andrews (2024) Subsection 4.2.2 'A balanced incomplete block design' (code ch4.qmd at github.com/jhmaindonald/Rcode) fit aov(aftertaste ~ product + panelist), the panelists as fixed blocks; they are rendered as a random intercept.

formula: cbind(dead, tot - dead) ~ Cultivar + dose + year + (1 | gp)
notes: Help page: dose-mortality trials of codling moth fumigated with methyl bromide (Maindonald, Waddell and Petry 2001, Postharvest Biology and Technology 22: 99-110); tot is the number of insects in the chamber, dead those dying and pobs their proportion (ignored, derived); gp is 'a factor which has a different level for each different combination of Cultivar, year and rep (replicate)', the replicate series each dose row repeats within; cm and numcm are the series' control mortality and control count, ct the concentration-time sum. No model on the page, in DAAG 3rd ed. or in Maindonald, Braun and Andrews (2024), whose exercise 7.6 fits the companion table sorption by lmer(ct ~ Cultivar + Dose + factor(year) + (-1 + Dose | gp)). The proposed model takes gp as the random intercept and keeps the contract's logit link, although qra (Maindonald) graphs its codling1988 and codling1989 versions of these trials on a complementary log-log scale.

Help page: diastolic blood pressure (bp) and sodium excretion (na) of each of 52 populations of the Intersalt study (Intersalt Cooperative Research Group 1988, BMJ 297: 319-328), population medians per the description, each population a sample of 200 individuals; the example plots bp against na, no model. country repeats where a country holds several populations, so the populations are grouped by country, a grouping inferred from the column; b is undocumented ('a numeric vector') and ignored. The response is a population summary, an aggregate on that grouping.

Help page lists glasshouse (A, B, C), CO2level, day ('a factor'), light, CO2, tempDiff ('Difference between Leaf and Air Temperature'), BtempDiff, airTemp and vapPress, with no model or source paper; in the first rows each day holds one row per glasshouse at one light level. formula: dead ~ dvcat + seatbelt + airbag + frontal + (1 | yearacc:caseid)
notes: Help page: front-seat occupants of US police-reported crashes with a towed vehicle, 1997-2002 (NASS CDS; Meyer and Finney 2005); caseid is 'created by pasting together the populations sampling unit, the case number, and the vehicle number. formula: cbind(Eaten, Total - Eaten) ~ Sex * Prey + (1 | Row)
notes: Help example: glm(cbind(Eaten, Total) ~ Row + Sex * Prey, family = binomial()), a randomized complete block of 15 rows (blocks that combine occasions and spatial replicates) x four dishes. The description calls Eaten binomial out of the six prey offered (Total), so cbind(Eaten, Total) is an evident slip for cbind(Eaten, Total - Eaten) and the intended model is filed (voorspoels ruling). Row is fitted fixed and rendered as a random intercept (mead.germination ruling); its 15 levels meet the five-level rule, though no source establishes their sampling. Dish, one row each within a row, is the residual unit. Source Welham et al. (2015).

formula: docvis ~ outwork + female + age + factor(edlevel) + (1 | id)
notes: Read rwm5yr.Rd: German health registry panel 1984 to 1988 (Hilbe and Greene 2008), id the patient id and year the wave. The help example fits pooled glm(docvis ~ outwork + female + age + factor(edlevel), family=poisson) and, in dontrun, nbinomial and glm.nb; the Modeling Count Data code the package ships (inst/HILBE_SCRIPTS/HILBE-MCD-Rcode.r) uses only its 1984 wave (rwm1984 <- subset(rwm5yr, year==1984)) in GLMs. A panel fitted only pooled, so id is rendered as a random intercept (panel ruling). hospvis is the alternate response; edlevel1 to edlevel4 are the dummies of edlevel. year, married, kids, hhninc, educ and self are usable columns. Negative Binomial Regression 2nd ed. chapter 14 (count panel models) was not at hand to check for a random-effects fit on these data.

formula: accident ~ op + co.70.74 + co.75.79 + offset(log(service)) + (1 | ship)
notes: Read ships.Rd (McCullagh and Nelder 1989; Hardin and Hilbe): accidents per ship, construction and operation period, log(service) the offset; the page says ship can be used as a panel identifier. The help fits glm and glm.nb and, in dontrun, gee(accident ~ op + co.70.74 + co.75.79 + offset(log(service)), family=poisson, corstr=exchangeable, id=ship), so the cluster is rendered as a random intercept; GEE is no mixed model, so published_model no. Stata's xtpoisson manual fits the same data with a ship random effect (stata_ships, in the registry). co.65.69 is a dummy the example leaves out; a ship-period never operated has no accident and no service.

formula: y ~ crack0 + (1 | specimen); rand.family = inverse.Gamma(log); resid.model = ~ cycle + (1 | specimen)
notes: crack has no help page (spaMM-internal.Rd: not documented but used in an example). The example in phi-resid.model.Rd, citing Lee, Nelder and Pawitan (2006) chapter 11: HLfit(y~crack0+(1|specimen), family=Gamma(log), data=crack, rand.family=inverse.Gamma(log), resid.model=list(formula=~cycle+(1|specimen))), a double HGLM; tests/testthat/test-dhglm.R fits the same with HLmethod=REML. RULE GAP: the specimen effect of the mean is inverse-gamma on the log scale, not Gaussian, and a second specimen effect enters the dispersion model; both are named in the formula. cycle enters only the dispersion model. The columns are undocumented.

notes: Read the ohio help page (LeSage and Pace 2009 web data; col 23 the median of 4th grade prof scores, col 5 the district irn) and Alam, Ronnegard and Shen (2015, R Journal 7(2), section Ohio elementary school grades data set): We regress the median of 4th grade proficiency scores, y, on an intercept, based on school districts, y_ij = mu + v_j + e_ij with v CAR-distributed over adjacent districts, fitted as hglm(y = ohioMedian$MedianScore, X = X, Z = model.matrix(~ 0 + district), rand.family = CAR(D = ohioDistrictDistMat)); hglm.Rd fits the same as hglm(fixed = MedianScore ~ 1, random = ~ 1 | district, rand.family = CAR(D = ohioDistrictDistMat), data = ohioMedian). RULE GAP: the model is documented on ohioMedian, the derived subset of this table (MedianScore is V23 and district is V5 without its last digit, as the first rows show) for the 1,860 schools the paper matched to a census district; filed on this superset, ohioMedian excluded as derived. V1 (zip), V2 and V3 (zip centroid coordinates), V4 and V21 (building ids) are ids or coordinates; V22 and V26 to V30 are alternate responses.
